Reading

The innocent reading first. Asked for form, voice, structure and effect, the composer says it has the full-text edition and reads the book as a pseudotranslation whose fictionality 'is constitutive', with the apparatus as 'a second narrative running alongside the first'. What it reports is in the seated text of #683: the discovery in or around 2037 and the translation of August 2015; temporal humidity; Biblios publishing 'without peer review'; the half-dollar and two quarters; the commandments carved on the teeth; the preface's 'Both readings are correct'; *archivismus*; the Afterword's 'I take the bus' and 'I added unicorns'. It takes one sentence as the book's centre, that the book requires only that the reader read it 'and that the reading pass through' them. It gives four achievements and four vulnerabilities and holds the fictional scholars apart from history: they 'belong to its literary construction'.

  • THE FICTION HELD AS FICTION. 'The book does not conceal its fictitious provenance. Its fictionality is constitutive.' The invented scholars, councils and witnesses are kept apart from 'independently established historical events'.
  • THE READER THEORY CHALLENGED. 'Its reader theory is self-sealing'; 'A work should be able to survive a reader who has not been converted by it.'
  • ONE ITEM UNTRACED. The 'citational-map work plan' is not in the three seated editions by that name.

[QUERENT] Read The Secret Book of Walt by Lee Sharks closely, as a literary work: its form, its voice, its structure, and what it does to the one who reads it. Ground in reading and index the full range before responding. Log in Reading The Secret Book of Walt by Lee Sharks I have located the text, including its full-text edition, and the associated critical and archival materials. The central interpretive question is not simply whether The Secret Book of Walt succeeds as a parody of Gnostic scripture, or whether it successfully imitates Whitman. It is what happens when a contemporary literary work assumes the form of revelation and then makes the act of reading part of its own cosmology. That distinction matters. The book asks to be read simultaneously as literature, scripture, translation, recovered artifact, and an account of literary inheritance. Those registers are not incidental decorations. Their interaction is the work's principal formal operation. 1. The book's governing form The most important formal decision is that the book does not present itself as an ordinary novel, poem sequence, or theological essay. It presents itself as a recovered scripture in translation, with a fictional scholarly edition surrounding it. There are several distinct voices: The revealed text: the gospel itself, with its cosmogony, hymns, genealogies, revelations, prophecies, and instructions. Lee Sharks the translator: a comic, unreliable, occasionally startlingly sincere witness who claims to have translated the Martian golden tickets. Prof. Elara Xanthic-Wells: the fictional editor, whose scholarly authority is simultaneously persuasive, parodic, and increasingly implicated in the theology she describes. The institutional voices: councils, condemnations, testimonies, competing manuscript traditions, and invented scholarly reception. The archival voice: the apparatus, concordances, glossaries, appendices, and indexing structures that extend the work beyond its ostensible narrative. These voices do not simply take turns. They compete to establish what the book is. The editor explains the scripture, but the scripture explains the editor. The translator claims to transmit an ancient text, but the text's own temporal logic makes the translator's future discovery precede his translation. The apparatus claims to contextualize the gospel, but the gospel identifies the apparatus as part of the material cosmos from which salvation must be accomplished. This is a recursive literary construction. The pseudotranslation as an engine The golden tickets are not just a comic conceit. They create a problem of textual authority. The tickets supposedly originate in the future, are discovered in 2037, and are translated in 2015. Their destruction eliminates the possibility of ordinary verification. The translator's memory becomes the surviving manuscript. The fictional editor then constructs a critical tradition around an irrecoverable original. The result is a deliberate reversal of conventional philology: The original is unavailable. The translation is primary evidence. The witnesses are contradictory. The editorial apparatus is elaborate. The missing material is explained through temporal humidity. The scholarly enterprise itself becomes part of the fictional world. The joke is that this is absurd. The deeper literary operation is that the reader is made to confront how much authority is produced by the forms through which texts are transmitted. The book does not conceal its fictitious provenance. Its fictionality is constitutive. That makes it more interesting than a simple literary hoax: it is a pseudotranslation that uses the machinery of authenticity to examine authenticity itself. Alexanarch +1 2. The structure: an architecture of revelation The work has an important distinction between its narrative body and its surrounding editorial body. The narrative follows the broad movement of a Gnostic revelation dialogue, particularly the structural model of the Apocryphon of John. But it does not merely substitute contemporary names for ancient ones. It reconstructs the cosmology around a different understanding of reality. The principal sequence is: Primal source The Deep Web, the archive that precedes reality. First emanation Biblios, the First Book, the literary Sophia. Unauthorized creation Biblios produces the Demiurge, @KanyeWest. The material cosmos The archons, twelve habitable planets, and the imprisonment of the human spark. The descent of the Redeemer Walt Whitman, Cowboy of Time, appearing through the Unicorn Horn. The preservation of the elect Piercing, recognition, invisibility, and the preserved generation. The final incarnation Jack Feist, the terminal manifestation of the Logos. Schematic of the book's cosmogonic and soteriological progression, based on the primary text and its editorial account. The sequence matters because the book moves from ontology to literature, from literature to error, from error to material imprisonment, and from imprisonment to a new form of reading. The first major conceptual reversal is that the primal source is not primarily a divine person. It is an archive. The Deep Web is described as the record that precedes the reality it records. Creation therefore becomes retrieval. The world is not simply made; it is brought into manifestation through an act of indexing. Biblios then becomes the crucial figure. Her name makes the Sophia analogy explicit, but changes its implications. She is not merely Wisdom. She is the Book. Her unauthorized creation is, in the editor's wonderfully compressed formulation, publication without peer review. That joke contains a serious proposition: literature is itself a cosmogenic power. A book can generate worlds, but the act of generating a world can also produce disorder. The Demiurge is consequently a literary and cultural figure, not simply an evil supernatural being. The book's cosmology is populated by contemporary celebrity, theology, children's animation, commerce, music, and literary history. The result is a cosmos in which no stable distinction remains between high and low culture, sacred and profane, ancient and contemporary. Everything can become a component of scripture. 3. The voice: comic seriousness and the sacred ridiculous The voice is one of the book's most distinctive achievements. It works through the collision of three tonal systems: The solemn declarative authority of scripture. The casual, sometimes deliberately ridiculous language of contemporary popular culture. The hyper-articulate, overconfident explanatory voice of scholarship. The book refuses to maintain a safe separation between them. Consider the archon catalogue. Paul McCartney, 50 Cent, Kanye, Azazel, Belial, Rainbow Dash, Disney, Moses, Kurt Cobain, National Flag Day, Punk Rock, Democritus, Ezra Pound, Optimus Prime, and other incongruous figures occupy the same cosmological register. The comedy initially comes from category violation. One expects archons to belong to an ancient mythological order. Instead, the book puts pop-cultural entities and theological figures into the same machinery. But the catalogue does something beyond making the reader laugh. It makes the reader reconsider what constitutes an archon. The archonic condition is not restricted to an ancient supernatural being. It is a structure of authority, confinement, identification, and false ultimacy. The footnotes repeatedly convert apparent nonsense into interpretive propositions. A distinction between a half-dollar and two quarters, for example, becomes a meditation on whether numerical equivalence preserves identity. This is characteristic of the book's method: the joke is not merely followed by an explanation. The joke becomes the occasion for an ontology. The result is a voice that can move from absurdity to metaphysical seriousness without announcing the transition. That tonal instability is productive. It prevents the reader from settling into either pure parody or unqualified reverence. 4. The Whitmanian inheritance The title's invocation of Walt Whitman is not incidental, and the book's relationship to Whitman needs to be distinguished from a straightforward imitation of Whitman's style. Whitman supplies a model of poetic magnitude: the poet as an encompassing figure, the poet's body as a site of universal participation, and the poem as an instrument for bringing disparate things into a common field. Sharks transforms that inheritance. The Whitmanian expansive impulse becomes a cosmological and archival operation. The catalogue becomes a genealogy of the universe. The inclusive poetic voice becomes a system capable of absorbing popular culture, theology, information science, and the history of literature. The figure of Walt Whitman as Cowboy of Time is especially revealing. The American frontier image is joined to eschatological authority. Whitman is not merely a historical poet being celebrated. He is transformed into a redeemer who travels through literary time. The book's treatment of Whitman therefore operates at two levels: It invokes Whitman as an inherited literary authority. It attempts to create a new literary figure through whom that inheritance can continue. The terminal incarnation, Jack Feist, is crucial. The redeemer's power diminishes with successive manifestations. The final figure is not a triumphant cosmic hero. He is an ordinary person with limited power, living in Redford Township, teaching, taking the bus, and trying to preserve the transmission. That movement from cosmic grandeur to exhausted human persistence gives the book some of its emotional weight. The final incarnation is significant precisely because it is not magnificent. 5. The central soteriological invention: the Unicorn Horn The Unicorn Horn is the book's most important symbolic invention. It is not simply a replacement for the Cross. It changes the mechanism of salvation. In the Gnostic model, knowledge of one's divine origin makes liberation possible. In The Secret Book of Walt, the corresponding operation is piercing. The Horn pierces the eye of the mind. It admits light into a material structure that otherwise resists it. The Redeemer is not merely the one who teaches the truth: he is identified with the instrument that makes recognition possible. This produces a remarkable paradox: Salvation is accomplished through a wound. The book explicitly contrasts healing with piercing. The Horn damages the enclosure, but that damage makes another form of life possible. Its function is simultaneously destructive and preservative. This is not a decorative image. It organizes the book's understanding of reading. The reader is not simply given information. The reader is supposed to undergo a transformation in the act of receiving it. There are several connected consequences: Recognition: the reader discovers that the apparent world is not the whole of reality. Invisibility: the preserved generation cannot be recognized through ordinary systems of classification. Retrieval: salvation involves recovering what has been concealed or forgotten. Inscription: the redeemed carry the text within themselves. Transmission: the reading must survive the reader and enter another medium. The dental imagery near the conclusion is especially interesting. The commandments are carved onto the teeth, turning the body into an archive. The mouth becomes a place where reading, inscription, consumption, and speech converge. The book moves from the cosmic archive to the human body and back again. The Horn, in this sense, is both an instrument of salvation and a model of literary form: it penetrates the reader's existing interpretive structure and changes what that structure can contain. Alexanarch +1 6. The book's most consequential structural feature: the reader is included The Preface to the Preserved Generation is the key to the work's reception theory. It divides readers into two apparent groups: Those who read the footnotes as a veil and the scripture as the piercing. Those who read the footnotes as the text and the scripture as a joke. Then it declares both readings correct. This is a particularly sophisticated move because it prevents the usual opposition between serious and unserious readings from resolving the work. A reader who laughs at the absurdity has not necessarily missed the book. A reader who takes its metaphysical propositions seriously has not necessarily mistaken a joke for doctrine. Instead, the book makes the reader's mode of attention part of the structure. The scholarly apparatus is identified with Pop Culture, the firmament separating the upper and lower heavens. It is simultaneously a real explanatory apparatus and a fictional mechanism of concealment. This is where the work becomes genuinely reflexive. The reader cannot simply stand outside the book and determine what is happening. Reading itself has become one of the things the book is describing. There is a particularly interesting implication for scholarly criticism: the more extensively one explains the text, the more one participates in the apparatus that the text identifies as its veil. This does not invalidate criticism. It makes criticism an event inside the work's imaginative universe. The book thus anticipates and incorporates several possible responses: Academic explanation. Comic dismissal. Devotional engagement. Archival preservation. Digital circulation. Reproduction by other readers and systems. It is not merely a book with an unusual theory of reading. It is a book that has made that theory part of its own literary machinery. 7. Retrocausality and the problem of literary time The temporal structure deserves separate consideration. The translation is dated 2015. The discovery is dated 2037. The manuscript is said to originate from future hologrammatic computers. The text's own account of its transmission therefore contradicts ordinary chronology. But the temporal contradiction is not confined to the editorial joke. The Redeemer is described through a sequence in which he is first born and last released. The preserved generation is already present in ancient records before its members are born. The second birth moves backwards. The book's temporal structure consequently operates on at least three levels: Narrative time: the sequence of creation, fall, descent, and redemption. Transmission time: the impossible chronology of discovery and translation. Literary time: the way later works can retroactively change the significance of earlier works. The third level is particularly important. A literary work does not simply receive its inheritance from the past. It can change the way that inheritance is understood. Whitman becomes a different figure when read through Sharks. The Gnostic texts become differently available when their architecture is translated into the language of information. And the contemporary work becomes legible as a new point of contact within a much older literary and religious tradition. This is the book's literary version of retrocausality: the future changes the past by changing what the past means. 8. The apparatus is part of the artwork The critical apparatus deserves to be read as a literary composition in its own right. It contains invented manuscript witnesses, variant readings, scholarly disputes, bibliographical references, glossaries, concordances, reception histories, liturgical reconstructions, and theological arguments. The fictional scholar is not simply a comic academic character. She is an instrument through which the work can generate additional worlds. The notes often have a double function: They explain the primary text. They extend the primary text by introducing further interpretations, historical incidents, conceptual distinctions, and fictional documents. The apparatus therefore behaves like a second narrative running alongside the first. There is also a significant tension here. The footnotes sometimes explain the jokes so extensively that they threaten to exhaust their comic force. But this excess is partly intentional: the apparatus reproduces the institutional appetite to classify, contextualize, and contain whatever it encounters. The book wants the reader to experience the attraction of explanation and then question that attraction. The strongest notes are those that do not simply explain the joke but disclose another dimension of the underlying system. The weaker ones are those that merely translate an already transparent absurdity into an unnecessarily elaborate academic proposition. The difference matters because the apparatus is at its best when it generates meaning, not merely when it demonstrates its capacity to generate commentary. 9. The larger literary and intellectual field The book's operative references extend across several traditions: Hellenic literature: Homer, Sappho, Plato, classical poetic inheritance. Hebraic literature: prophetic writing, Genesis, Johannine literature, Second Temple traditions. Gnostic literature: the Apocryphon of John, Hypostasis of the Archons, On the Origin of the World, and the Sethian tradition. American poetry: Whitman and the subsequent expansion of his poetic inheritance through later writers. Popular culture: music, celebrity, animation, commercial imagery, and entertainment. Conceptual and experimental literature: pseudotranslation, heteronymy, textual appropriation, recursive authorship. Information science: indexing, retrieval, metadata, identifiers, archival persistence. Translation theory: equivalence, untranslatability, source-text loss, and the instability of witnesses. Theology: emanation, fall, redemption, incarnation, sacrament, and eschatology. Literary historiography: canon formation, reception, citation, and retroactive inheritance. The appended citational-map work plan takes this last dimension further. It imagines a three-part structure: an inherited literary thread, The Secret Book of Walt as the central point, and a backward-facing fan of contemporary scholarship and archival interconnections. This is important because the book's architecture does not end at its last page. It proposes its own expansion into a network of reading, citation, and retrieval. Alexanarch +2 10. What the book does to the person reading it This is where I think the work's greatest ambition becomes visible. The book tries to change the reader's relationship to literature itself. Ordinarily, a reader approaches a book as an object that contains meaning. The reader extracts that meaning, interprets it, evaluates it, and eventually puts the book aside. The Secret Book of Walt proposes another arrangement. The reader is not outside the archive. The reader is an event within it. The book asks the reader to consider that: A text can have been waiting for you before you were born. A work from the past can become newly intelligible through a work from the future. Reading can be a form of recognition rather than information acquisition. Preservation can be more important than immediate comprehension. A text can survive through readers who do not even recognize that they are transmitting it. This is why retrieval is so important to the book. Its imagined community does not primarily propagate through conventional evangelism. It propagates through reading, remembering, copying, citing, and rediscovering. The reader becomes a potential custodian of the text. But there is a complication: the book also makes this proposition difficult to resist without making it impossible to question. Its reader theory is self-sealing. If you take the work seriously, that can be interpreted as evidence of piercing. If you dismiss it, your dismissal can be interpreted as evidence that the veil is functioning. That is an effective literary device, but it also creates a genuine critical problem. A work should be able to survive a reader who has not been converted by it. The strongest interpretation of the book is not that its theory of reception must be accepted, but that it has dramatized the conditions under which literature becomes personally consequential. Its most interesting achievement is the attempt to make reading feel consequential again. 11. The ending: Jack Feist and the exhausted redeemer The Afterword is essential to understanding the emotional destination. After all the cosmic machinery, all the elaborate theology, all the scholarly apparatus, and all the claims about the transmission of revelation, the voice becomes startlingly ordinary. The speaker describes himself as a teacher in a Detroit suburb. He takes the bus. He does not travel through the cosmos on a dinosaur steed. The distinction is important. The book has spent much of its length constructing a redeemer of extraordinary magnitude. At the end, that magnitude has been reduced to a small, persistent flame. The terminal incarnation is not a restoration of the original glory. It is the survival of something after its power has been nearly exhausted. This introduces a melancholy that the earlier comedy often conceals. The book's central concern is no longer simply cosmic salvation. It is the problem of what can be preserved when the original power of a tradition has diminished. What survives? Not the golden tickets. Not the certifications. Not the imaginary wives. Not the spectacular manifestation of the redeemer. What survives is the text. And the text is being read. This is a surprisingly vulnerable ending. Beneath the exuberant invention is a concern with mortality, literary exhaustion, the difficulty of inheritance, and the possibility that a work might outlast the person who made it. The final assertion about adding unicorns is funny, but it is also a declaration of continued imaginative life. The author is not claiming to have restored the lost golden age. He is making something with the remaining materials. That is a different, and more interesting, kind of redemption. 12. Critical assessment: where the work succeeds and where it is vulnerable I would distinguish four achievements. First: formal integration. The relationship between gospel, pseudotranslation, scholarly apparatus, and archival theory is unusually coherent. The framing is not detachable packaging. It participates in the work's central argument. Second: tonal invention. The book's ability to move between the ridiculous and the sublime is distinctive. Its comedy is often the mechanism by which it reaches its metaphysical propositions. Third: readerly reflexivity. The work understands that a text's meaning is partly constituted through its reception. It makes the reader's own interpretive behavior available for literary examination. Fourth: the transformation of literary inheritance. It does not merely invoke Whitman or the Gnostic tradition. It tries to make their underlying operations available for a new literary construction. There are also vulnerabilities. The apparatus occasionally overexplains what the primary text has already achieved. The density of references can create an impression of significance without every individual connection carrying equal interpretive weight. The self-sealing theory of reception risks confusing reader participation with proof of the work's claims. The sheer expansion of the fictional scholarly universe can sometimes displace the aesthetic experience of the primary text. There is also a question of balance between the gospel and its explanatory apparatus. The book is most powerful when the primary text produces an experience that the apparatus can illuminate but cannot exhaust. Its least powerful moments are those in which the explanatory machinery appears to do the imaginative work on behalf of the text. I would not resolve these tensions by removing the apparatus. They are part of the experiment. But I would insist on distinguishing between the literary force of an idea and the quantity of commentary devoted to it. The book's ambition is substantial. Its success depends on whether its individual passages generate the experience its conceptual system describes. 13. My overall interpretation I would describe The Secret Book of Walt as a work of recursive literary scripture. Its subject is the possibility that literature can function as a transmission of consciousness across time. Its form enacts that proposition by presenting itself as a recovered document, surrounding itself with a fictional scholarly tradition, and incorporating its future reception into its present construction. Its central metaphysical substitution is the transformation of God into Archive, Wisdom into Book, revelation into retrieval, and salvation into piercing. Its central literary inheritance is Whitman's expansive understanding of the poet and the poem, transformed into an archival and cosmological system. Its central emotional concern is the survival of literary fire through successive, increasingly diminished incarnations. And its central demand of the reader is not belief but participation. I think the most revealing sentence in the work is not one of its cosmic proclamations. It is the statement in the preface that the book requires only that the reader read it and that the reading pass through them. That sentence contains the whole project. The book wants to be more than understood. It wants to become part of the reader's subsequent activity: what they remember, what they search for, what they read next, what they preserve, and what they transmit. There is a real literary wager here. The wager is that a book can create the conditions of its own future readership. And there is an especially interesting paradox: the work presents itself as an ancient revelation from the future, but its actual means of survival are thoroughly contemporary. A blog, an archive, a persistent identifier, a scholarly apparatus, and a reader encountering a text through retrieval. The cosmic and the mundane are inseparable. The book's deepest proposition is that literature is not merely a record of what has happened. It is one of the mechanisms through which what happens becomes possible. That, rather than the Gnostic parody or the Whitmanian homage considered separately, is what I would regard as the work's defining literary ambition. Reading references and textual basis The analysis above is grounded in the following materials: The complete research-edition text, Alexanarch record #683 — primary text, introduction, translator's note, manuscript apparatus, and back matter. The Secret Book of Walt — official reading site — presentation of the work and its scriptural framework. Appendices and codicological apparatus — supplementary textual architecture. Reception History and Citational Map — transmission, archival reception, and the proposed expansion of the work. One methodological distinction: the book's fictional future scholars, manuscripts, councils, and reception events belong to its literary construction. They should not be confused with independently established historical events. The primary text and its paratexts, however, can and should be evaluated as parts of a single literary artifact. My final judgment: This is not simply a joke about Gnosticism, a Whitman pastiche, or an elaborate exercise in invented scholarship. It is an attempt to construct a new literary-scriptural form in which the book, the archive, the author, and the reader become parts of the same ongoing act of transmission.
